newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa gold output seen plateauing at 500 tonnes.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa gold output seen plateauing at 500 tonnes.

text.p: The decline in South African gold output is expected to bottom out with production in the medium term seen holding around 500 tonnes a year, the Minerals Bureau said in its annual review.
Gold production in South Africa, the world biggest producer of the yellow metal, has been dropping steadily in the past decade due to increasing costs and decreasing recovery grades.
Production has dropped from 640 tonnes in 1986 to 522.4 tonnes in 1995 and the Chamber of Mines said late last year it expected the industry to produce only 490-495 tonnes of gold in 1996.
The 1996 production year promises to be the worst since 1956 with output half that produced in 1970 and some six percent down on 1995 production.

"The dramatic production declines of 1994 and 1995 are not expected to continue, though a drop to around 500 tonnes per annum is anticipated for the medium term from 1996," said the bureau -- part of the department of mineral and energy affairs.
It said revenue from gold sales is expected to increase by only 6.6 percent from 26 billion rand in 1996 to 27.7 billion rand in 2001.
The Chamber of Mines released November gold output figures in December showing a miniscule improvement in November production to 41.68 tonnes compared to October's 41.09 tonnes.
The industry's gold output for 1996 to November was 450.6 tonnes compared to 1995's 478.0 tonnes -- a 5.7 percent decline.
The bureau said the financial position of South Africa's gold mines will strenghten in the short term through the effects of the rand currency's drop against the dollar but added:

"Inflationary pressures created by the weaker currency will negate these advantages in time. The mines will thus remain under pressure and further restructuring of the industry in response to the ongoing profit squeeze can be expected".
South Africa's gold mines are the deepest in the world, with some reaching more than three kilometres underground, making gold recovery very expensive and dangerous.

But the country still holds around 40 percent of the world's indentified gold reserves and the world's largest gold miner, Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, said last year it was investigating two new ultra deep mines which could see gold mined up to five km below the earth's surface.
